Item agreed to.
St. John harbour-improvements, $500,000.

This amount of
$500,000 is required for improvements in St. John harbour. It is intended to complete the dredging of a channel from the main channel in St. John harbour to the basin in front of the drydock, a distance of about 7,200 feet in length by 500 feet wide, to a uniform depth of 22 feet and to complete the dredging of the basin in front of the drydock to a depth of 32 feet, as well as dredging a channel 250 feet wide from' the basin to the drydock. It is also required to complete a contract with
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

Messrs. Boone & Macdonald for the construction of a conveyer gallery 1,100 feet long, with necessary equipment at berth 16; for general maintenance of harbour, repairs to sheds, wharves, conveyers, and so on. At West St. John it is intended to protect concrete exposed to sea action and at Partridge island to repair the wharf. There is also dredging in shoal areas in the main channel to a depth of 32 feet, and dredging the deep water berths. These constitute the main undertakings.
I understand that Courtenay bay at St. John is a new harbour. How much has been spent on the work there?

A breakwater has been constructed and we have been dredging the entrance to the harbour. This is to complete the dredging programme. This is all preliminary to the work to be done in connection with the piers and the facilities that will 'be required to make the harbour a proper terminus.
This is not for Courtenay bay?

No; it is for
dredging outside the bay. The estimated cost at Courtenay bay is $5,184,600, and the total cost to date is $4,771,000, extending over a period of years between 1918-19 and 1924-25.
Has the minister the figures showing the total amount spent on St. John harbour up to date? I think it will be interesting to the committee to see how much these harbours cost.
There has been a total expenditure of $19,000,000 on St. John harbour dating back from 1874 to the present time.
That does not include the dry-dock?
Yes.
What was the cost of the dry-dock?
Has the minister any figures regarding the total tonnage through St. John? Is there any revenue collected from the harbour?

Yes, there are
some revenues collected by the Marine department who are administering the wharves. The city collect revenue; they have some property there as well.
I am not interested in the city. What does the government collect?
I have not the totals here.
Does the minister not think it would be wise to have a harbour commission, or some way of collecting dues at St. John?
The regular port dues are charged there and collected.
Are they expected to pay on the basis of the interest on the loans made to them?

No, the regular
port charges collected in other ports such as St. John are collected there. It is not a regular harbour commission. The Marine and Fisheries department have their agent there who collects the dues on the tonnage of the ships as they come to and go from the harbour. In addition to that the city collects revenue from their property.
We would have to find out from the Department of Marine what revenue is collected there.
Yes, they would have that information.

The dues charged and collected at St. John harbour have been rather exorbitant in the view of the shipping people. Last year the city fathers decided to cut down their tolls because they were driving ships to the United States ports down along the eastern coast. I think possibly the Marine department charges were correspondingly high. Is it the intention of the department to do anything on the Negro point breakwater this year?

That whole situation is being very carefully canvassed now with the transportation companies, the city and the engineering department. The question of further development in St. John I think requires very careful consideration, and the whole matter is being carefully gone into.
Will this vote complete the harbour work at St. John and Courtenay bay?
No.

What will be required to
complete it?

It depends on
the plan adopted. If the Courtenay bay scheme were proceeded with to the full extent it would mean a large expenditure. If there should be developments which we are trying

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
to arrange I think a very large sum could be saved, and that matter is under consideration now with a view to saving money if we *can.

Does the government not
think it advisable to look over the situation and call a halt in the matter of great expenditures and future developments? I do not think the commerce of the country would suffer one io'ta if we cut out seven-tenths of the expenditure which we have been making; we would be in a much better position financially, and it would give a great *deal of hope to the Canadian people who are under a burden at the present time.

Is there any congestion at
the port of St. John at the present time?

Not at this
season of the year. It is a winter port, and in the winter time they suffer from congestion. In regard to the tonnage last year, 14.000 head of cattle were shipped and I think eight or nine million bushels of wheat passed through. In addition to that there was a great deal of produce and other merchandise.

I think under present conditions the government should go very slowly in regard to spending a large amount of money on ports in the east. We have to provide duplicate facilities in the east to handle our business, and I think they could very well put up with a little congestion at times in order to cut down expenses, especially when we are up against the conditions which exist at the present time.

We have that in
mind.

I was in St. John a year ago, and Courtenay bay looked to me like a new project that was being undertaken. If you are going to develop that info a new port it is going to take an immense amount of money and will only be used a few months in the year. Then we have to go up to Montreal and Quebec and provide another set of facilities in those places. I think the government would be well advised if they would proceed very slowly in commencing any projects of 'this nature.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 147, page 36. All the items in this estimate have been passed except two, Escuminac and Mill's point. Mr. Kellner moves that the vote for Escuminac, harbour improvements, $50,000, be reduced by $49,500. The question is on the amendment of Mr. Kellner.

This is a new
structure required in the interests of a large fishing community, to give them the protection which they need in their occupation.
I trust that the hon. member will withdraw his amendment. I do not think he wants the people of this community to be deprived of that which is necessary to enable them to earn their livelihood.
How much will be ultimately required for this work?

Not any more
than this.

I Understand from one who.
lives down there that there are only about twenty-five families in the whole neighbourhood. We can spend $50,000 for about twenty-five families, but we have over three-quarters of a million people in Saskatchewan and we get $17,000. There is something wrong. Talk about putting nails in the coffin of confederation; I think you are doing it at a good rate.

The value of the salmon fisheries there is $90,000, employing forty to fifty boats. As to what my hon. friend has said about the population, I would point out that the many boats operating there indicate a very fair population. Salmon,
herring and lobster fishing is carried on by some seventy boats drawing three and a half feet of water, and fifty dories. The population is 1,780.

Throughout all the estimates of this kind this year there has been a tremendous discrimination as between different provinces. When you think of $21,000 being spent for public works in the whole of Saskatchewan you cannot blame the mover of the amendment (Mr. Kellner) for his feeling in the matter. I am surprised that when the Prime Minister visited that part of the country last year the significance of this condition did not strike him rather forcibly. For many years we have had at Saskatoon a half-finished building, the completion of which would save $22,000 annually in rent. We are paying to-day in rent an amount which, capitalized would provide accommodation in our own building, and it would be a credit to the city. The minister eulogizes the beauty of things east, particularly around this city, but all these matters should bear some relation to each other, and at present I cannot see that they do. I do not wonder that there is discontent in the west, and some of the legislation that has lately been put through this parliament is not calculated to allay it.

I think our western
friends hardly realize that such expenditures as these are to communities in the Maritime provinces what branch line railway construction is to the west. If a comparison is made between the amount spent in railway building, repairs to wharves, harbour works, and so on, in the west and in the Maritime provinces, the large expenditure would not be found to be in the Maritime provinces. My riding does not touch the coast at any point, but I krfow a good deal about the conditions at such places as this. Communities such as this situated along the coast of the Maritime provinces have only one method of communication largely, and that is by boat, and if they do not have wharves and harbours in to which they can put for shelter in a storm, they are in great danger of loss of life and of property in the way of boats and gear. I think it comes with a pretty poor grace from our western friends, who are so keen for branch line construction, to oppose a small vote of this kind which is to provide communication for people who live in sections where the people have less opportunity to make a living than almost in any other part of Canada, and where they are more out of touch with the outside world. I am going

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
to vote against the amendment to cut this vote. I think there are votes that should be cut out, but I do not think this is one of them.

I am glad to have the support of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) in conection with this vote. I do not think the people of the west fully appreciate what the fishermen along the eastern coast have to put up with and the hardships they endure. They have no railway communication at this point, being forty to forty-five miles away from a railway, and after making their catch the fish has to be transported by steamers and motor boats and motor trucks for that distance to put into freezers or shipped by rail. It is a very hazardous coast. Miramichi bay is accessible and fairly safe for large craft, but when a storm comes up, these drifters, of which there are a large number going out every day when the weather is favourable have to put in, and they are very chary about venturing out whenever they see signs of a storm approaching. Two years ago, I remember, there was a great deal of excitement on acount of the boats being out during a storm. I think I mentioned that when this vote was up before, and since then I have received a letter from home saying that one young man lost his life during that storm, and the other boy was able to stick to the boat and was picked up later and brought to shore. The boat equipment is worth $3,000, and every boat carries almost a mile of nets, and instead of these boats going out three or four miles, as I said before, they go out fifteen or sixteen miles from point Escuminac. Hon. members will readily realize the hazardous nature of this calling. I believe that this extra expenditure will increase the trade at this point. Last year their catch of fish amounted to $400,-
000.
Some statement was made when this vote was up before to the effect that this kind of fishing had been carried on for a great many years and that it could be done with comparative safety, but the fact is that fishing in these drifters has been carried on only during the last eight years; I have that from fishermen in the district. About 400 men are employed at Escuminac, going out fishing for lobsters and salmon, and there are men who come up from the north shore and fish there along with the others. These men also require a safe port to put into. People also come up there from the coast of Prince Edward Island and up north into Gloucester county, and at the present time they would have to run to Shippigan or Prince Edward
Island if a storm came up. One boat has foundered during a very severe storm with all hands, since the last debate we had on this vote.
I know you people from the west will appreciate the difficulties we have in the Maritime provinces. We have a feeling down there that certain portions of Canada are opposing any appropriations that would help us build up our trade, and this is one of the appropriations that we feel would very materially assist us in the Maritime provinces, and especially at that point in New Brunswick, to develop our fishing trade to a far greater extent than at present. Every fish that we take out of the Atlantic is of advantage to the Canadian people, so I hope that when this vote comes before you, you will unanimously pass this item of $50,000 for a breakwater at Escuminac, and that the hon. member will withdraw his amendment.

I do not think any member of this House would oppose a vote for this purpose if he really thought this work was absolutely necessary for the protection of the fishermen. It is a large amount of money, but at the same time I do not feel like voting against the appropriation. I am perfectly sure that those who have supported this amendment are quite serious, believing that the money should not be spent, but I cannot see my way at this time to support the amendment.

It is very hard to hear
of so many fatalities down in that district, but I want to point out that if people persist in going on the water there will always be a certain number get wet and a few others get drowned. When this vote came up in the House before, there was not one argument given in support of the need of this particular work. The whole statement as presented in the House was that it was to pay for a by-election. That is what was presented to the House. I know absolutely nothing about the situation myself. I do not know whether this work is necessary or not,, but if that charge was not correct, I think it was up to the hon. member to have got up at that time and defended the vote.
I want to take exception to my hon. friend's statement. I did defend the vote, as he will see if he reads my remarks in Hansard.

Not until I had moved
the amendment. I moved the amendment to test this House, to see if they had the
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

courage of their convictions, as several had spoken against the vote, and they claimed it was not required at all. I have no information about the district myself. I do not know whether this work is needed or not, and we have not been given any reason for it.

I objected to this vote when it was up before, and I intend to do so again. I had a talk with the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Snowball) following the last debate, and he failed to convince me that this large vote was required, or was in keeping with the economy talk we have heard so much of in this House. I made the statement on the last occasion this vote was up that there was a greater coast line in the constituency I represent than in any constituency in the Maritime provinces-200 miles and more; and that we produced more fish in that constituency than in any constituency in the Maritime provinces. Since then I have looked up the records to verify my statement, and I find I could have doubled that statement. I can safely say that there is more fish produced in the constituency I represent than in any two constituencies in the Maritime provinces, and the records of the department will prove that; yet in my constituency there has been spent only $9,700 on public wharves in the last thirty years, and we axe producing fish by the hundreds of carloads.

Are there any deep
sea fisheries in your constituency?

There are deep lake fisheries; we have very large lakes, but, of course, we do not have so many by-elections out there. I have made some private investigations regarding this matter, and I find there are about twenty-five families in the immediate vicinity of Escuminac-I have been told this on what I take to be excellent authority- who will be served directly by this work. I understand also that it is more of an experiment, that later on there will be another $150,000 expended' on this work. I state again, I do not think it is dignified for this House to launch out on an expenditure of $50,000 to satisfy the obsession of a few people. Speaking on this question before, I remarked that it was hereditary with the people of the Maritime provinces-
Order, order.
Why the point of order? In what I said there was nothing derogatory of the people of the Maritime provinces. It is my intention to oppose this vote.

I do not want to vote a
sum of $50,000 unless we know what we are doing.

It is $200,000
altogether.
You can vote against it.

I shall do what I think is
right n& matter what advice is given to me by other hon. members. I should like some information as to the necessity for this particular expenditure. It is all very well for the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) to compare lake shores with the Atlantic ocean, but the two axe not comparable. I think I have complained about votes for harbours on the Atlantic as much as anyone, and in the present case I should like to know the extent to which this particular community will be benefited by this expenditure.

I have a letter from
W. S. Loggie & Company in which they say "this breakwater is absolutely necessary." This firm is one of the largest producers of fish in that section.
How much fish is produced there?	.
Fish to the amount of $400,000 was produced in the locality last year.

Is there any possibility that
more fishing will foe done if this improvement is carried out?

Yes, more fishing will
be done.

I have not heard the
discussion, but I think anyone who accepts an assurance on the information we have from the minister-I heard the previous discussion and I do not presume there is any more information now-is very easily satisfied. Does anybody imagine this House is justified in launching on a $200,000 expenditure-for that is what it is, with another dock nearby and all the dredging that has to be provided for under another vote besides the $200,000 we are embarking upon now-and that in relation to a parish where in 1921 the whole population to be served by both works, was some 1,700-probably less now than more-and where only a few of these people will be engaged in fishing? I do not doubt there is some purpose behind this, but is that purpose sufficient to launch us upon an expenditure

Elections Act
which will probably involve $400,000 by the time the dredging is taken care of and the two docks built? Is it conceivable? I think it is inconceivable. The fact oif the matter is that it is an affront to the House to ask us to discuss it.	*
Amendment (Mir. Kellner) negatived: Yeas 32, Nays 77.
Item agreed to on division.
Mill's Point-wharf enlargement and repairs, $25,000.

This is a supplementary
by-election item in the same county? This is at a point that nobody has ever heard of and cannot find on the map. Is not this in Northumberland county too?
This amount is for the reconstruction of a wharf. The expenditure is a proper one, there is no question about it.

Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State) moved that the House go into committee on Bill 148, to amend the Dominion Elections Act.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-urban polling divisions.
Will the minister state shortly what we are really doing?

This is to increase the population of an urban polling division. When the act was first passed the population was placed at 1.000. In 1921 an amendment was passed making it 2,500. The present amendment fixes the number at 5,000.

What is the
reason for the change?

My hon. friend will find it in
the marginal note which reads:
As originally passed in 1920 the act required urban registration in all places having a population of 1,000 or more. At the next following session it was amended by increasing the lower limit to 2,500 the effect being thus to reduce from 440 to about 185 the number of places in which personal registration was required. Neither the public interest or the convenience of candidates would seem likely to be in any way prejudiced if this limit were still further raised. On the other hand its being so would relieve some voters of a burden ana would effect a substantial economy since the number of revising officers would be reduced and the printing of some lists would be dispensed with.
It tends to economy and improved administration of the act.
This really means, I suppose, that the rural machinery, for example, as to swearing yourself in and that sort of thing on the list, applies to a greater number than before.
Yes.
What is supposed to be the economy in that? What is the difference?

The number of revising officers will be one thing and the printing of the lists another. The urban lists have to be printed and the rural lists do not. The explanatory note by the Chief Electoral Officer gives the reasons why the changes are made. He gives the illustration:
If, for example, the lower 'limit was increased to 5,000, the number of places in which urban registration was essential would be reduced by over 55 per cent, viz: from about 185 to 80. There are some few places with populations between 2,500 and 5,000 which, as is presently true of some places under 2,500, would still require urban registration. For example, the population of St. Lambert, West Toronto, and like municipalities adjacent to large cities, and of some towns in Western Canada, are too flued to permit the intimacy upon which the effectiveness of rural registration ultimately depends. Urban registration would have to be directed in these in the same way as it is now directed in Oak Bay near Victoria, in South Vancouver, and in St. James near Winnipeg, but a population of 5,000 is, in general, quite low enough to make urban registration essential.
How is it decided when you rely on your 5,000 and when you are going to do something else?
Under the act it is left entirely to the Chief Electoral Officer to do that at the time.
What principle is to guide the officer in determining whether we are to be rural or urban in the absence of a declaration of parliament?
No principle is definitely laid down by statute. Under the act it is left entirely to the Chief Electoral Officer to decide those questions as they arise during the election.
Is the object to be attained chiefly the saving of expense?

Yes, and to relieve the necessity for registration.

Elections Act

Is there
not a little danger in throwing too wide open this swearing in on polling day?

It will add only a few more.
They would have the same opportunity of doing it now, but it would make a larger number of rural constituencies and there would be an opportunity to swear in if necessary. It is a matter which has been decided upon after careful consideration and after the Chief Electoral Officer has had the experience of administration under the old act.

I am very apprehensive of this clause. It means, as far as I can see its practical effect, . that the places where heretofore a person couid go in and swear his name on and vote on election day are multiplied several time3. Heretofore, a voter, without going on a list or coming before a judge, without the slightest precaution being taken as respects him, in a town of 2,500 or under could walk in and swear that he had a right to vote, and if he got outside of the door, you would never hear of him any more. It is very difficult to do that illegally and fraudulently in small places, because everybody there knows everybody else. But when you get a place with a population of over 2,500 and up to 5.000, the difficulty ol detection is multiplied, and in my judgment this is just opening the door to wholesale fraud and to swearing in of voters on election day who come from no man knows where. Why do we not do this in the large cities? Just because it would mean a torrent of " telegraphers " and every other kind of thug coming in and swearing in their votes. A whole army could not watch them. If we are going to open the door up to towns with a population of 5,000, to my mind it is going to degrade the whole election of our country, and that is pretty hard to do. It is getting now, especially in our cities, something unspeakable. I have the gravest suspicion of a bill of this kind and especially of this subclause (1). It is all very well to talk about saving a little expense, but what is this going to amount to? It will multiply the places where this swearing can be done, and that means .throwing open the widest possible door to fraud. This does not usually occur in the small places although it has been taken advantage of there. You will usually find the whole voters' list taken up by somebody even in a small place. But in a place with a population of over 2,500, it is impossible to check this thing and, in my judgment, the legislation is vicious.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would remind the House of a long-settled practice, that where a private bill has been considered by a special committee, the report of that committee is sustained by the House unless some good reason is given to the contrary. Special committees are supposed to consider very carefully the bills submitted to them and to go into all details concerning those bill's before they arrive at the conclusions which they recommend the House to adopt. I know nothing whatever of the particulars of this case-

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL

speechtext:
-but I am free to say that I think if the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) were in his seat he would support the view which I am asserting, that this House would make a great mistake if on the ipse dixit of any member it should disregard the report of a special committee.

Calgary and Fernie Railway

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, is the hon. gentleman sponsoring this bill sure that the directors whose names he read are still alive?
I have been given to understand that it is nineteen years since the company first got its charter, and that in the interval all the original directors have died.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: The only information I have is that which I gave from the telegram. Mr. Hough is one of the prominent barristers and solicitors of Winnipeg and a man of the highest reputation. If he is dead, he has died within the last day or two. The telegram is signed by his firm, Hough, Campbell & Ferguson, and I am quite sure that any statement contained in it is true, because that firm would not lend its name to anything that was not true.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: As we have not heard from these gentlemen for nineteen years, is it not to be presumed that they are dead?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: They cannot be dead if they present a petition to parliament.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I opposed this bill before the special committee, and I am opposing it here. If we must abide by the decision of a special committee, as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) suggests-

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: My hon. friend is not correct. I simply said that the usual practice was for the House to accept the report of a special committee that has investigated any bill unless some special circumstances were shown to the contrary.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman is correct, then the question naturally occurs to me, what is the use of parliament? Let us have matters considered entirely by special committees and save our time in the House. For example, if the hon. gentleman's view is correct, the Church Union Bill should not have been discussed in the House at all because the special committee which considered it came to a very decided conclusion in the matter. Despite what he says, I think it is the right of this House to examine very carefully every application which seeks to renew the charter of any corporation which has not carried out the conditions on which its charter was granted. Now, this charter was granted in 1906-exactly nineteen years ago -and has been renewed every two years. It has been said that plans have been filed and that certain work has been undertaken in connection with the building of a road on that portion of the line extending up the Elk valley from Fernie. The line is proposed to
be built from Calgary southward, crossing the Rocky mountains by the Kananaskis pass, and then down the Elk valley to the city of Fernie, B.C., a distance approximately of 150 miles. It is true that preliminary location plans have been filed with the Department of Railways and Canals. Hon. gentlemen will understand that these are not the final plans on which a railway company builds. I do not know how it was done, but the map filed, with all its contours and so on, looks to me as if it had been prepared by the Interior department, the route having merely been drawn in to indicate the approximate course of the proposed railway line. Several extensions of the charter having been granted, in . 1912 the railway company made application to be granted a subsidy by the Dominion government under the provisions of the Subsidies Act, which act received the royal assent on April 1, 1912. Hon. gentlemen will recall that under that legislation a double subsidy was provided for, dependent upon the cost. The initial subsidy was $3,200 per mile, and under certain conditions that amount might be increased to a maximum of $6,400. The Calgary and Fernie company came under the provisions of that act, and I am going to read to the House part of the discussion in connection with the subsidy as reported in Hansard of 1911-12 at page 6329, volume 4:
43. To the Calgary and Fernie Railway Company, for a line of railway from a point at or near the city of Calgary, in the province of Alberta, in a southerly direction via Kananaskis pass and the head waters of the Elk river to cr towards the city of Fernie, in the province of British Columbia; not exceeding one hundred miles.
Hon. gentlemen will recall my mentioning that the line was supposed to be 150 miles in length, but apparently the subsidy was granted only to the extent of 100 miles. Then the following discussion took place between Mr. Oliver-the Hon. Frank Oliver, former Minis er of the Interior, now a member of the railway commission-and Mr. Cochrane, then Minister of Railways:
Mr. Oliver: What is the tota/1 distance from Calgary to Fernie?
Mr. Cochrane: The total 'length of the line will be 150 miles. I do not know whether that takes in the whole distance or not.
Mr. Oliver: Is this Calgary and Fernie Railway Company a subsidiary company of the Canadian Pacific Railway?
Mr. Cochrane: I never heard that.
Mr. Oliver: Has. the company a federal charter?
Mr. Cochrane: Yes.
Mr. Oliver:	How long has the company had a
charter?
Mr. Cochrane: Since 1906.
Mr. Oliver: How many renewals have they had?
Mr. Cochrane: The company has given us the assurance that they will start right in on construction.

Calgary and Fertile Railway
I desire to remind members that this is a discussion which took place in the House of Commons on March 27, 1912, and I would emphasize that statement made by Mr. Cochrane: "The company has given us the assurance that they will start right in on construction."
Mr. Oliver: Might I ask what is to be the policy of the minister in granting these subsidies? We are glad to see subsidies granted, and we want the roads constructed, but when a subsidy is granted on the assurance of the company that it is going on to do the work, will that subsidy itself be withdrawn and the rights of the company cancelled if they do not proceed with the work, and the way thereby cleared for some other company to go on with the construction?
Mr. Cochrane: There is a good deal in what the hon. gentleman says. The matter has been discussed across the floor of the House between the ex-Minister of Railways and myself, and while, perhaps, in every case, it should not be done, I think as a general policy it is a good thing. It wfM shut off charter speculation.
Mr. Oliver: Up to the present time this has been clearly a purely speculative charter.
That, is the observation of the Hon. Frank Oliver to the then Minister of Railways, and that statement was made thirteen years ago.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: There has been a war since then.

speechtext:
I am glad to have the assurance of the hon. gentleman in that regard. To continue:
Mr. Cochrane: We will give them this chance, and if they do no^ go on and construct we will say goodbye to them.

speechtext: Question! _

speechtext:
I do not propose to let the
hen. gentleman interfere with my argument for a single moment with any observations he may ni3ke of that character. Though his mind may be closed, I will read again for the benefit of those who may pot have caught the significance of Mr. Cochrane's observations just what he said:	.
Mr. Cochrane: We will give them this chance, and if they do not go on and construct we will say goodbye to them.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: What did he mean by that -"we will say good-bye to them?"

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
I take it in view of the context which I have already read that what Mr. Cochrane meant was that unless this company got on with the construction work, the company was going to be eliminated and that so far as its charter was concerned it would be taken away from them.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the situation that existed in 1912. Since that time this company has done nothing except file the biennial applications for charter renewal. I venture to say that not a single dollar outside of the legal expenses and the expenses

incident to these applications to parliament has been spent since that occasion, and certainly I am quite sure that is true of the time previous to that.
Now in 1923 this company paade applications for a further extension. At that time in the Railway committee I suggested that the two years would elapse, and in my judgment the application would be renewed for a further charter life without the expenditure of a single dollar. The application has been made. The representative of the company has admitted that not a single dollar has been spent in the interim and now this further application is made to parliament for the purpose of getting the imprimatur of this parliament to this further speculative venture.
The matter has received the attention of a considerable number of people in western Canada. The territory which this railway is supposed to traverse is a very desirable territory. The territory immediately southwest of Calgary is largely a farming country. Then there are not only oil fields further south between Calgary and the mountains, but in addition to that there is a considerable prospect of further oil development. I may say to hon. gentlemen for their information that one company alone is producing 300 barrels of oil a day from the natural gas which is there found. The mountain area is largely underlaid with coal, a variety of coal which is of exceptional value, being described I think by geologists as semi-anthracite, and considered as among the best of the varieties of coal we have in Alberta. There are several coal companies in there which have made considerable development. I know, for example, that Mr. P. Burns has a very larre area of land, and he has gone to a great deal of expense in trying out and testing the coal area. On the other side of the mountains I am informed there are considerable forest areas, and that the lumbering industry would probably be valuable in that area. Now the people are anxious to have these areas developed. They are satisfied that they never will be developed so far as this railway company is concerned; they are satisfied this company will never put the railway through. It is the view of a great many that this is simply a speculative charter. We could not find out in the Railway committee the day before yesterday who the directors were. The gentleman representing the corporation simply told us they had spent 5200,000, just when or where or how was not quite clear. He could not tell us the name of a single director, and yet in

Calgary and Fernie Railway
the face of that the Minister of National Defence tells us that the Railway committee has carefully considered this application, and has placed its seal of approval upon this charter.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
I said
nothing of the kind. I said that that was the duty of the committee, and it was to be assumed that the committee did that.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: My hon. friend got up and asked the committee to pass this charter willy-nilly, and now I am telling him that as a matter of fact the representative of the company the day before yesterday in the Railway committee was unable to give the name of a single director. He told us all the information he had was that $200,000 had been expended, just when or where or how he did not know.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me, I am a member of that committee, and I wish to say that the particulars as to directors were given to the committee. I would not have voted in favour of the bill if the conditions had been as the hon. gentleman represents them to be.
Mr. iSHAW:	Was the hon. gtentleman
present at the Railway committee meeting?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I was.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) who made the inquiry did not get the information.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: If he did not get it, I got it.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: My recollection is that not the name of a single director was presented to the committee by that gentleman.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Have you got that information now?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I have the information from the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson).

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Then what are you kicking about?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: -who read from a wire he just recently received apparently from Winnipeg.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but I do not want him to represent things in the Railway committee as he is doing before this House, as if the members of the Railway committee were absolutely absurd and ridiculous and voted for things they knew nothing about.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: It is not- my duty to make any reflections on the Railway committee.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: You had better not.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I am not afraid to; don't worry about that.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: We are not absolutely stupid!

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Would the hon. member please read the letter which the solicitor who appeared before the committee said he had furnished him w'ith, or that Mr. Hough had furnished him with, giving full particulars?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I am glad the hon. gentleman has directed attention to that. The gentleman representing the company suggested that a letter had been written to me by Mr. Hough a lawyer of Winnipeg in connection with this matter. I would like this committee to know that the letter was written two years ago at the time this charter renewal was up. I suggested then that there was no possibility of this company doing any work, and I asked Mr. Hough who was here then representing the company to give me a letter which would satisfy me that they really intended to do something, and in the letter-I speak entirely from recollection and from the observations made by the representative of the company in the Railway committee-it was pointed out that $135,000, not $200,000 had been spent. It was also pointed out that the money was available over in England; that all they needed was the granting of a charier and money was coming, oceans of it, for the purpose of carrying out this venture. I ask the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy) if he is satisfied with the bona fides of this company? After the statements presented to me upon which I relied, and upon which I think I had a right to rely, I did not raise any objection, although I was urged to make objections to the passage of the bill at that time, and I withheld my hand, having faith in the observations which were made to me by the gentleman associated with the bar at Winnipeg.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: At that time you received this definite assurance that all they required was the renewal of the charter and that oceans of money would come from England to complete the work? Has any work been undertaken in the two years that have elapsed?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
No, I think that is admitted by the representative of the company. No work whatever has been undertaken in the
Calgary and Fernie Railway

last two years, indeed for years past. Now, this matter has been under consideration by various people in western Canada, and I want to give the committee the benefit of their observations. These people are on the ground and know the situation. I think if parliament wants to do its duty it should pay due respect to the requests which they make I have a letter from the city clerk of Calgary, under date of March 31 of this year, in which he writes to me as follows:
Dear Sir,
He. Calgary and Fernie Railroad Charter
At the regular meeting of council, held last evening, a communication from the secretary treasurer of the Union of Canadian Municipalities was placed before the council for its consideration. This communication pointed out that the Calgary and Fernie railroad company was again applying for an extension of time in connection with their charter for the construction of this line. It appears that the original charter for this railroad was granted in 1906, and a series of ten extensions have taken place up to the present time.
I just interject here that I think, as a matter of fact, eleven extensions have been granted.
In this connection the city council passed the following resolution, and instructed me to forward copy of it for your information, in order that you may be able to advance the city's wishes when same is brought before the House:
"That this Council go on record as being opposed to any further extension of the charter of the Calgary and Fernie railway."
That, Mr. Chairman, is the considered view-the unanimous and considered yiew- of the city council of Calgary. But, sir, I do not rely entirely upon the observations in this regard made by the council of that city. I have in my hand a letter written by a farmer of the district to which I referred immediately south of Calgary. He points out numerous facts-I will not take up the time of the committee by drawing attention to them-with regard to valuable areas of agricultural and mining lands through which this railway will pass. He ends up by saying:
The charter of the proposed railway has been in existence since 1906, and has already had eleven extensions, and since the prospects of this company building. or even starting to build, are very remote, the settlers urge the recision of the charter to give another corporation the opportunity of applying for a charter and getting started to build a road of which we are in need.
I have a further. letter signed on behalf of the Fernie Board of Trade by J. Fred Spalding, secretary, to the following effect:
There have been persistent rumors during the past two .years that commencement was to be made at once. None of them however have brought a commencement anti apparently it is just as far off now as it ever was.
May I read now, a letter received by me from an ex-mayor of the city of Fernie? As I

have already suggested to the committee. Fernie is the southern terminus of this railway. The gentleman is Mr. Henderson, and under date of June 9, of this year, he writes as follows:
I am informed that that Calgary-Fernie Railway Company is applying for a renewal of its charter for a further period.
I have lived in Fernie for the last twenty-five years, and am thoroughly familiar with the local situation. I acted as mayor of the city of Fernie during the years 1920 to 1924, and at the present time am the police magistrate there, so that I have had the fullest opportunity of knowing intimately the facts in connection with the railway proposed to be bui'lt by the Calgary-Fernie Railway Company.
This railway was intended to be built down the Elk valley and thence into Fernie. A provincial wagon road extending forty miles north of Michel (20 miles east of Fernie) had been built up the Elk valley. I have travelled on this road and have not seen the si ghtest evidence of any railway work whatever being undertaken in this valley.
Two years ago, at the time when this company was applying for an extension of their charter, we were informed that the company had a large sum of money available, and that as soon as the charter extension, then applied for, was granted work would be promptly undertaken. It was also suggested that one Broley by name had the contract for this proposed work. No one seriously expected that anything whatever would be done and in the intervening two years I am quite certain that not a single dollar has been expended on this railway.
Under the circumstances, and in view of the many renewals which have been granted to this company, I do not personally think the charter should be extended.
Yours very truly,
G. G. Henderson.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there you have the considered views of public organizations, of Mr. Henderson, and of a .very reputable farmer in that district who speaks, or purports to speak, on behalf of the farming community south of Calgary. I think it would be very unwise, in view of the statements which I have made, in view of the facts that have been elicited in connection with the application, for parliament to again renew the charter of this corporation. I venture to say that two years from now this company will again come to parliament asking for a further renewal, that in the intervening time not a single dollar will be spent. More than that, I am satisfied this company is simply holding the charter. Mind you, I do not blame them for getting away with it if parliament is foolish enough to grant this extension, but I do not think it is.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order.
The hon. member has no right to say that parliament is foolish. It may be, but the hon. member has no right to say it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will use the word "unwise."

Calgary and Fernie Railway

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I did not suggest that parliament was foolish, I suggested that parliament would not be so foolish as to grant this extension, and that despite the views of the hon. member for Quebec South. What I want to convey to the committee is this: Here you have representative men, representative organizations, the Board of Trade of Fernie and the Calgary city council disapproving of a further charter extension. In view of those representations, in view of the fact that the charter has been renewed since 1906, in view of the fact that, although they were entitled to a subsidy, they never got nor claimed a single dollar under that subsidy arrangement, is it wise for this parliament to renew the charter? I believe the charter should not be renewed, and parliament will be remiss in its duty if it seeks to place a further extension of the charter into the hands of those who are interested for speculative purposes in promoting their own interests. Therefore, I seriously and sincerely ask the committee not to approve this bill.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
know of any company or corporation ready and willing to advance the money and construct the line within the next two years, or would it be his intention to have it constructed, like many other western branch lines, by the Canadian National Railways?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
I have no objection, if the
Canadian National Railways want to undertake the work and they are satisfied that it is a legitimate and proper enterprise, that they should be given a privilege in that field. That would be the logical thing to do. The hon. gentleman has asked me whether or not there is any other corporation ready to do the work. That is his test as to what this parliament should do-go on doing a bad thing because there is no organization in sight, so far as we know, which will undertake the construction of that particular railway. That is not the test at all. How do we know how many organizations or corporations there may be that, if they were not prevented from entering this field by 'this charter, would be willing to undertake the work.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Is this charter a monopoly? Does it exclude other companies?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
In law it does not, but in
fact it has that effect. My hon. friend shakes his head; but if he will refer to the discussions that took place in 1912 just on the particular subsidy arrangement I have spoken about, he will find it is clearly set out there-

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
If it carried a subsidy,
it would, but without a subsidy, it would not.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Is it at
all likely that any other company or group of men would undertake to ask for a charter? Does the hon. member think parliament would even grant a charter in this same area so long as this charter stood?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bow
River has probably made much clearer than I could the exact situation. No company will venture into that field with an already existing charter. They will be forced practically to 'buy out this particular charter.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Why buy it out?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: That is the only practical solution of the situation so far as they are concerned. I should like to remind my hon. friend that only the location plans have been filed, and the result is that this company can vary its construction within a certain radius, I do not know what it is. That is, their construction plans may be within a certain area.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Is this an exclusive charter?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Nobody suggested that it
was; but I am telling my hon. friend, if he will have patience, the exact situation. The fact is that these railway charters, when granted in this way, have the effect of keeping other legitimate railway corporations out of the field.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I was not present when this bill was before the committee. What reasons were advanced by the advocates of the bill why they were unable to go ahead?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Two years ago when the
matter came up in the Railway committee, the company stated that nothing stood in the way; that the money was available in England; that all they needed was for parliament to grant the extension and then the work would promptly proceed. I think they also said at that time that the work had been contracted for to this man Broley, this man of straw apparently, in Fernie, according to the statement of ex-Mayor Henderson. This time I understand the difficulty to be, if I caught it correctly, that money exchange conditions, with whicn they must have been thoroughly familiar when they made the application to parliament in 1923, had militated against their getting the money on anything like favourable terms. That is what I gathered as the reason given.

Calgary and Fernie Railway

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Is this the first renewal?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
No. The company was
granted this charter in 1906. This is the eleventh or twelfth extension. We must treat these matters seriously./ If we are going to grant charters to quasi-public corporations of this character, let us do so seriously. Let us not undertake to promote any speculative enterprise, whether it suits private interests or not.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Can the hon. member state any private or public interest which would be hurt by the granting of the renewal of this charter?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
I do not know that I could
undertake of my own knowledge to mention any public or private interest. The interests of parliament, more than any other, will be hurt. Parliament should not lend itself to speculative charter renewals of this character. We should seriously view our obligations in this regard and give life only to legitimate enterprises. I use the word " legitimate ", not offensively, but to distinguish a speculative enterprise from one that contemplates actually undertaking the particular work.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: Now that it is almost nine o'clock, will the hon. member be kind enough to tell us just why he is opposed to the granting of this charter?

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext: I fear the hon. gentleman was not in the chamber when I explained the matter, and I would1 not like to take time in order to explain it for his information.

maintopic: THE CALGARY AND EERNIE RAILWAY COMPANY BILL
speechtext:
Coming from a constituency which this railway, in part, proposes to traverse, I feel it is my duty to oppose the renewal of this charter. The people who live in the district where this road 9 p.m. is proposed to be built have, I think, given up any hope they may have had of the promoters of this enterprise ever building a railroad . The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) pointed out that the original charter was granted in 1906, and if these gentlemen had had the faintest intention of doing anything with their charter in the way of constructing a railway, they certainly would have some road constructed by this time. In answer to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), I would say that if this charter is granted, in my opinion it practically grants the exclusive right to build a railway through this territory. It traverses a hilly or mountainous country nearly all the way from Calgary to '

Fernie, and the railway must follow the route which naturally lends itself to railway construction.
