The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 148, to amend the Dominion Elections Act, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Urban polling divisions.

At six o'clock I was about
to offer some remarks in support of those made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in which he opposed the amendment which substitutes, for 2,509, 5,000 electors to be registered in rural polls. The reasons given by the leader of the opposition seem to me to be conclusive. It is all very well in rural districts to allow people to come in on election day and after taking the oath to vote. But in districts of any size one man may not know his neighbour, and particularly is he not permitted to know his neighbour's wife; so that the chances are very great of a large number of fraudulent votes being polled. It seems to me that the proper course for the committee to take would be to leave the 2,500 in the bill. In a village or municipality of 2,500. people, I can quite understand that the citizens would be known to one another; but in any place very much larger I greatly fear that the way would be left open to abuse. Particularly would this be so in municipalities, towns or villages situated adjacent to large cities where there is a more or less moving population. I think that possibly the chief electoral officer in making the recommendation contained in this section did not consider the matter carefully. Evidently he had too great trust in human nature and was not aware of the extent to which certain people carry their patriotism and their desire to help the country's business through their willingness to vote more often perhaps than the law considers judicious.

I want to add my
objection to those advanced to this section. It is, I think, opening up a chance for abuse in the running of elections and the government would be well advised to leave the section as it was before. Having had experience in two elections T know something of

Elections Act
the tactics of those at least who were my opponents, and even with the act as it stood before I found that they were able to poll votes in two and sometimes in three places. I do not think that the door should be left open at all to abuse in this direction.

I feel like those who have
objected to the section. It is true that I was a member of the committee that considered the bill, but the circumstances were such that I was unable to attend the sittings and therefore I am more free to object to this section than if I had sanctioned it in the committee. It was with a good deal of hesitancy that we permitted into the Elections Act the principle of swearing in voters, but I am quite willing to admit that there are some advantage to this where it is used under proper safeguards. Certainly it has the effect of ensuring that men and women otherwise entitled to vote shall not be deprived of the opportunity of voting. In the last election there were many instances that came under my notice where names had been left off the list or where they were not properly on the list through some inadvertence on the part of the officers. But the fact that these men and women were allowed to be sworn in at the proper polls on election day secured them the privilege of which they would have been deprived otherwise. That is a perfectly safe practice in rural districts where everybody is known to everybody else, but I am sure that it would be unwise to extend the present provision any further.

Does the hon. member not
think that in towns of less than 5,000 everyone knows everyone else?
No.

That is the case in my
town.

Twenty-five hundred is a
reasonable limit.

There is a good deal to be said in favour of the amendment, which was carefully considered by the committee. In answer to the objections that have been made, I would remind hon. members that the person being sworn in must be vouched for by someone whose name is on the list; both parties must be sworn before any vote can be registered by the person whose name does not appear on the list. Let us see the difference betwen rural and urban registration. Under the law as it existed before, in any municipality of over 2,500, any person desiring
to have his or her name put on the list must personally appear before the registrar, and that involves a great deal of trouble as well as considerable expense to those responsible for the registration. There are many voters, particularly since women have been given the privilege of voting, who are not in a position to go to the town hall, or wherever the registrar keeps office, for the purpose of having his or her name recorded. And unless that is done the person whose name is omitted may not vote in an urban district. In the rural district, on the contrary, it is the business of the enumerator to go from house to house to secure all names and put them on the list, and if a name is omitted in a rural district then the vote may be sworn in as indicated. Now, by extending this same practice to municipalities of any population up to 5,000 we are overcoming a great deal of difficulty; we are getting rid of a good deal of work on the part of those responsible for the registration and are not opening any door to fraud at all. After all, a municipality of 5,000 is comparatively small; and as I have already pointed out, no one may vote on election day unless vouched for by somebody whose name is on the list. If this section is adopted it will reduce trouble and expense in connection with registration; it will obviate the inconvenience to which the law as it now stands gives rise; and it will enable a great many people who otherwise would not be able to vote to take advantage of the ballot. In view of all these considerations and others that might be urged, I think it is wise indeed to extend the scope of the section and put the maximum at 5,000 instead of 2,500.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Newspapers, etc., required to disclose by whom articles, etc., having reference to an election, are paid.

There should
be an elaborate explanation, in the eloquent language of the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp), of what all this mass of English is supposed to mean.

Section 5 of the original act provides:
Every printed advertisement, handbill, placard, poster or dodger having reference to any election shall bear upon its face the name and address of its printer and publisher, and any person printing, publishing, distributing or posting up, or causing to be printed, published, distributed or posted up, any such document unless it bears upon its face such name and address is guilty of an offence against this act punishable on summary conviction as in this act provided.
Elections Act

It is proposed by the present amendment to repeal that subsection 5 and add a number of subsections to it, so that newspapers or other publications publishing election matter, cartoons or other election documents, which are described as election matter-
I suggest to the hon. minister that he take it section by section, and when he is dealing with the first clause will he say what a future candidate is, and how he may be defined?
I point to my hon. friend. In all probability he is a future candidate.
I am the present candidate.
Present representative.
The woods are full of them.

I submit that this section as proposed is bound to cause an immense amount of difficulty, inconvenience and uncertainty among candidates. It appears to me that section 5 of the act as it stands affords a reasonable measure of protection, because all documents must bear the name of the printer and the office where they are printed; so that it is pretty easy to obtain that information, and there is a measure of responsibility in the source of these documents. The section which is proposed in place of this simple section which now appears in the act is very complicated and involved. It is difficult for even a lawyer trained in interpretation to understand it. I do not profess to understand it, although I have spent a good deal of time trying to do so. I know there will be many candidates who will have greater difficulty than I had in interpreting it. Many of them will not be able to understand it at all. I am afraid it will cause a great deal of trouble, and compliance with it will be practically impossible.

I read this section and I must confess when I got to the end of it I had no idea what the beginning was about, and I thought perhaps it was due to my density, until I heard my hon. friend who has just spoken, who admits he is a lawyer, claim that he did not understand it. Under those circumstances I think it is about time to go back to the simpler language of the original rlause. If a lawyer who was on the committee and has been studying the proceedings before that committee and listening to the explanations of the electoral officer cannot understand this section, surely it would not be inter-

preted properly by any ordinary candidate who has not a. legal mind to apply to this clause.

I move that we strike out section 3 of this act, which leaves section 5 as it stands at present in the Elections Act.
Mr. MEIG-HEN: Is the minister who is sponsoring the bill not able to tell us what this jumble of words means? I direct his attention to the first few lines which read:
Election matter includes every reference or comment expressed or indicated in words or pictures, to or upon the selection of a candidate or candidates at any election the character, action or policy of any past, present or future candidate or candidates, the conduct or anticipated conduct of the supporters of any candidate or candidates the administration of any election or any subject in issue or suggested as being or having been in issue at any election.
Then the exception is still more marvellous than the sweep of the first inclusive clause, it says:
But shall not include references or comments of a historical or literary character-
My goodness, that is everything. What comment would there be that would not be of a literary character? Of course it might be of an "illiterary" character.
To of upon past events of notices-
That word "of" should be "or", I think.
Or notices or advertisements of future meetings containing nothing calculated to affect opinion.
The latter exceptions are understandable, but that first exception would to my mind wipe out all that was ever in it.

The draft of the bill was
brought before the committee on Privileges and Elections and we had several meetings in connection with it. The original section of the act was thought not advisable, and the committee asked the officers to draft a section that would cover as nearly as possible what would be in the interests of the carrying on of the election, so that everything would be properly considered in regard to advertising in newspapers and periodicals of the country.
In the present act there is a short clause in regard to this matter, and it was felt that newspapers and periodicals of all characters, which are using their columns for the purpose of advertising election matters on behalf of any candidate, should be asked to give to the public the information as to who is paying for it, whether it be the candidate himself or somebody on behalf of the candidate, corporations or otherwise. So far as

Elections Act
the government is concerned, we only desired to get some amendments to the Elections Act, and all of these amendments with the exception of one or two, were advised by the Chief Electoral Officer in charge of the administration of the act. I am not particularly wedded to this section or any particular section of the bill, but I am simply desirous of getting the best election -act we can in the interests of the proper conduct of elections in the future. This section might be studied a little more. My hon. friend was a member of the committee where this matter was very carefully considered, and it may not be just as complicated as it looks on its face. However. we might let that section stand and go on with some of the others.

Will the minister have pity on the committee and point out what it means? Will he tell us what he is trying to do? Will he tell us what the penalties mean and why the election of a candidate would be void under subsection 7 if the newspaper contractor does not file his affidavit? I would like him to tell me that from the act.

I do not think that could be
the intention.

Why not? The
reason I ask the question is because it was put up to me by one of the members who has been working hard to try and find out what it was. I told him that in my view it referred only to where the publication was printed. He retorted, "Well, you prepare the notices yourself, you revise them after they have been typewitten, and then you give them ,to the newspaper, but if the newspaper does not file the affidavit you become liable for a non-indictable offence and punishable on summary conviction." Does 'the government really want to do that?

Mr. Chairman,
I would point out the effect of subsection (6) and (7). Subsection (6) reads:
When any publication other than a periodical contains *any election matter, there shall appear on the title page or the face of the publication a statement showing the name and address of the persons who have paid or agreed to pay the expense of the issue or distribution of such publication,-
Let us assume a candidate wishes to distribute some memorandum to his workers, he will have to insert on the front page a statement that it is to be paid for by himself. If that is not done, subsection (7) provides the penalty, and it goes even further:
(7) If in any periodical or other publication any election matter is inserted or appears contrary to the provisions of this section, or without the statement hereby required, every one who prepared or revised the copy for such election matter, the owner or owners, and the publisher of such periodical, every one who has received or become entitled to receive payment under any contract for the printing of such other publication, every one who has distributed, posted up or exhibited or caused to be distributed, posted up or exhibited such other publication, and every one who, with knowledge that it contains election matter, has distributed such periodical, shall be guilty of a non-indictable offence under this act punishable on summary conviction as in this act provided.
New if any candidate acting in the best of faith prepares any pamphlet or document and distributes it to his workers or any body does it on 'his behalf, and it does not contain this statement, |or the act has not been complied with, he is liable to a penalty. It seems an absurdity.

Mr. Chairman, I was a
member of this committee, but was only able to attend one of its meetings owing to their clashing with the meetings of other committees. I never saw the section before; if I had I would have opposed it. This section is really wonderful. If any reference were made either to Sir John A. Macdonald or Sir Wilfrid Laurier in any newspaper published in the Dominion, as both of them come under the definition of "candidate" as given in the Elections Act of 1920, the publisher responsible would be liable to one year's imprisonment, with or without hard labour, if he had not filed the required affidavit with the Secretary of State. In my opinion there is no escape from that. conclusion. I submit that if any member of this House, be he lawyer or layman, reads this section five and comes to the conclusion that it means anything else than what I have stated, the committee might entertain it; but frankly, within my experience I have never seen such a piece of draftsmanship.

If there is any particular objection to the clause on the ground of its being unreasonable or unworkable, I am willing to withdraw it. It was discussed very carefully in committee and recommended to the House for consideration.

Have any abuses developed
that- would make necessary such a drastic provision as is here proposed?
I do not know of any definite cases.

Mr. Chairman, section 3 of the original bill was not satisfactory to the committee, and it was left to the Chief Electoral Officer to draft another seiction to take its place. For my part, I cannot see that the new section is any more acceptable
Elections Act

than the original. Perhaps the Secretary of State can tell us of something that has happened at elections in the past which makes this section necessry.

I have not any definite cases
in regard to it.
Amendment (Mr. Stewart, Leeds) agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, at this
point I desire to move an amendment to a section with which the bill does not deal, and I think it will come most fittingly at this point. It is a very simple amendment in these words:
That the bill be amended by inserting the fallowing
as section 3:	,
Subsection (1) of section 10 of the said act is amended by inserting the words "or a labour union" after the word "alone" in the third line thereof.
Hon, members will recall that I introduced an amendment to the Elections Act early in the session asking that sections ten and eleven be repealed. I ask that section ten be repealed on the ground that it imposed an undue hardship on labour unions, inasmuch as they are prohibited, except they are incorporated for political purposes, from contributing to election funds. The amendment was defeated. I am now asking that labour unions be excepted from that prohibition. If my amendment carries, section ten would then read:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone or a labour union shall, directly or indirectly, contribute,
and so on. I do not think it is necesary for me further to explain this amendment. I debated it early in the session. I would urge that inasmuch as it does not appear to be the intention of those who drafted the original act to impose any hardship on labour unions, this committee would do well bo remove the prohibition by passing the amendment which I have proposed.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order According to the hon. gentleman's statement, early this session he made an attempt to amend the Elections Act along the lines which he is proposing now, and he was then defeated. Under the rule he cannot bring the same subject twice before parliament in the same session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
member where was the former amendment submitted? By what body was it dealt with?

The bill referred to was
dealt with by this parliament at the beginning of this session. It provided for the repeal of section 10 which I now ask to amend. I

do not however, think this amendment is out of order, inasmuch as it adds a phrase, while the bill moved previously was drawn to repeal the whole section.

My recollection of the occurrence is that the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) introduced a bill to accomplish the pfirpose he now seeks to accomplish, and the hon. Solicitor General suggested, I think, that the matter should be dropped as amendments were in contemplation to the Elections Act and that that would be the appropriate time at which to present his proposal.
Was not the bill defeated? The member himself said it was.

I rather think he is in error
in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why diould an exception be made of labour unions any more than any other unions, the Manufacturers' Association, for instance, or any other organization of that character?

The answer to that is that
the minister, or those around him at least, objected to the proposed amendment brought in earlier which made no exception of any class. I am not anxious to get a privilege for labour. I would like to see the whole section repealed. I do not want the Manufacturers' Association, for instance, to be prohibited from contributing to election funds. Why*should they not contribute? The whole-section assumes that elections in this country can be won by the power of money. I do not believe they can be won by money, in western Canada at all events, but I do say they cannot be won without money, and you are making it very difficult for one section of the community to collect any -money for this purpose. I say this section can be got around, and that you have here an act which compels people to be criminal. What is the use of keeping a Stupid thing like that on the statute book? Why not remove it?

I have considerable
sj'mpathy with the attitude of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine). I think myself the act is too restrictive, too detailed, too multiplied in its definition of crimes and offences, and after this bill goes through it is going to be far more so. Under our Elections Act to-day, if you print a bill, if you pay something that is quite legitimate and forget about it, if you wear a red ribbon or a blue ribbon or a red tie, in fact, if you do anything

Elections Act
except stand in an attitude of prayer you have got to go to the penitentiary. The fact of the matter is we have legislated everything into a crime in connection with an election until if a man were to study the act for half a lifetime he could not possibly comply with it. He could not do it.
Nobody does.

Nobody does, with the
result that not only are those acts which a normal man would consider quite legitimate perpetrated day in and day out, but the most brazen offences are perpetrated. What I rose to say is this:	If instead of these minute
provisions which we solemnly pass just as if they were never to be looked at again, we would make it the duty of the general returning officer to see that there is some decent obedience paid to sensible provisions, make him an administrative officer, and not let it be possible again for hordes of "telegraphers," impersonators and all manner of beings to rush from poll to poll and put votes in from morning to night, with all sorts of affidavits taken that are not affidavits at all, with judges signing certificates without ever seeing what is in them, signing purely blank papers- in a word making the whole act a farce at the hands of subordinate election officers'-if it were made the duty of the general returning officer to look after these things, instead of the mere watching and legal supervision of some sort of proclamation and the posting of it up at the right time, then we would get some results from the act as it is. I would like to see the general returning officer made responsible for the fair decent conduct of elections, and not just be merely a sort of law clerk watching the legal administration of the technical provisions of a very involved statute.
There may be some clauses of this bill that are unobjectionable, perhaps some that may be useful, but from what I have seen of it so far, it is simply fussing away about little things we really do not need to bother about, while the great big offences are allowed to go unscathed.

Personally I have no
objection to section 10, which makes it a criminal offence for the Manufacturers' Association and any similar organization or union contributing to political funds being withdrawn altogether. I was glad to hear the leader of the opposition speak as he did, because if I recollect rightly that section was inserted during his regime, and we were just a little suspicious in the wrest at that time as 
to the purpose for which it was put in the
act.
What section?

The section making it an
offence to contribute to political funds.
Oh yes, I think we were super-virtuous.
I do not wish to make any lengthy remarks. I am glad to support the suggestion of the hon. member for East Calgary.

With regard to section 10
being put in the act under the regime of the leader of the opposition, it is true there was in the act that preceded this a clause that had reference to contributions by certain business organizations, but the change that was made in the wording when this amendment was inserted with reference to associations incorporated for political purposes alone, left the, impression on our minds that the change was designed to affect the farmers' organizations in the west, which were then beginning to have a great deal of influence. It is true we got over the difficulty by incorporating ourselves after a great deal of trouble, for political purposes, thus achieving the end we had in view. It put us in the position of doing what we were doing perfectly openly, while the large corporation could do all' they wanted to do in that way and yet keep it entirely secret.
Personally I have no objection to the whole thing being wiped out. I have no objection to the Manufacturers' Association contributing money for political purposes if they see fit to do it, and they do do it, and all the other organizations do it, and I do not see how it is possible for us to provide an act that will stop it. As regards the farmers' organization they were put to a great deal of trouble and difficulty and had to devise ways and means of getting over the act.
Oh, oh.

We did not get over it,
we simply incorporated for political purposes only in order to comply with the law, but it put us to a great deal of trouble and unnecessary expense. As far as the money spent in our constituencies is concerned, I know it does not all appear in the statements that are made to the electoral officers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should like to deal with the point of order, unless some other hon. member desires to speak on it.
Elections Act

Mr. ME1GHEN: I did not know there was one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes. The point of order has been raised that the amendment moved by Mr. Irvine, having been voted on in the House and dealt with, the question cannot be re-introduced at the same sitting.
In regard to the point of order, can you tell the House whether the motion was agreed to or withdrawn?
I raised the point of order on the statement made by the hon. member for East Calgary himself.
Was the motion defeated?
It was defeated.

Speaking to the point of
order, I should like to point out that the bill introduced by the hon. member for East Calgary proposed to wipe out in their entirety sections 10 and 11 of the Elections Act. The amendment which he now proposes is to insert a few words in the existing section 10. It cannot be said that this particular matter has previously received the consideration of the House.

I should like also to say a word on the point of order. I am not very particular whether or not the amendment was withdrawn previously or voted down by the House, but I claim that the motion made by the hon. member for East Calgary is not in order because it is not an amendment to the bill now before us. The bill which the committee is now considering is Bill No. 148, an Act to amend the Dominion Elections Act, and while any hon. member has the right to make an amendment to any clause contained in this bill, the fact that the hon. Secretary oif State brings down an amendment, or three or four amendments, to the Elections Act does not give an hon. member the right to propose any amendment he may desire to make to the original act and oblige tne members of this House to vote upon a measure which otherwise that hon. gentleman would be obliged to introduce as a public bill. I contend that the amendments to this bill must be relevant to the measure as introduced, as read a first and second time, and as now on the table for consideration, and that any amendment to any other clause of the Elections Act is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I feel that this question is not the same as the one previously
[The Chairman.]
dealt with. Bill No. 5, as introduced by the hon. member for East Calgary, provided:
That sections 10 and 11 of the Dominion Elections Act, chapter 46 of the statutes of 1920 are repealed.
That is the whole bill, and that bill was negatived on February 19, 1925. This is not the same question by any means because it provides for the insertion of certain other words. I am inclined to think that this amendment is relevant because it deals with the right of corporations to make contributions. It seems to me, therefore, that it comes within the rule as to relevancy.

I should like a ruling on the point I have raised. That is on the question of relevancy to this bill. Many of the clubs had sums of money, not large, it is true, some $150, and others lesser amounts, which they would gladly have contributed to the campaign fund had they legally been able to do so, but they were unable. I want to say here quite frankly I believe in class organization, and class representation in the houses of parliament. I think there 
is not any use in trying to stem the current that is carrying us on, and if we can honestly and above board make it as easy as possible for different organized groups to contribute to campaign funds, we are not standing iD the way of progress, but rather aiding it, and for that reason I am in hearty support of the subamendment.

I want to make myself
clear to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Caldwell). I was not suggesting at all that his election funds were improperly raised. I merely wanted to point out that if he had used his organization to contribute he was in error and was liable to punishment. In the west we used the organizations. Supposing I had to drive over two hundred miles to collect 25 cents from two hundred farmers; why, it would cost me a fortune.

My people gladly sent
the m-oney in.

There is no need in building an organization you cannot use. I just wanted to point out to my hon. friend what my idea was in asking the question. I did not want to suggest that his funds were raised improperly at all.

I think the main thing is to
secure publicity. I fancy from what the hon. member for South Sim-coe IMjr. Boys) has vread from the act, that that is fairly well secured under section 79. I do not care whether the Manufacturers' Association or any other organization contributes for campaign purposes so long as we know who it is that is contributing, and what is the amount. While the purpose for which section 10 was placed here is no doubt a good one, I do not think it is effective or of any use, as far as I can see, and I would just as soon run chances on getting rid of it and try it out, so long as we have the publicity.

You would never get

Elections Act
On section 4-Appointment of returning officer.

Before proceeding with section 4 I wish to move an amendment as section 3A. This amendment has reference to section 12 of the act, which declares that no team, carriage, cart, vehicle, and so forth, can be hired by a candidate or his agent for the purpose of conveying electors to or from the polls. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) declare a few moments ago that in the application of the Elections Act he does not believe in shams. The Secretary of State has said that this law might be too stringent, but I submit to the committee that section 12 as it exists is practically impossible of application. That was the situation when only men were allowed to vote; it will be more difficult of application now that women also have the right to exercise the franchise. I ask hon. members who have had experience in electioneering whether or not outside of their own knowledge-because had they known it they might have been disqualified -it is not the practice for friends to hire cabs, wagons, automobiles, and so on, to carry electors to the polls on election day. It will be said, perhaps, that this provision of the law has been on the statute book for a long time. For the information of those who might find relief in the length of time this provision has been in force, I would like to state that it was enacted in 1874. At that time the English electoral law declared that it was not illegal to convey electors to the poles. Notwithstanding that-for reasons which we have not to account for now- fifty years ago this provision was embodied in the law. What has been the result of this legislation? I respectfully submit that it has not been carried out and cannot be carried out. It has been more difficult to enforce the law during the past four or five years since the right to vote has been granted to women. Does anyone believe that it is possible for women to get to the polls on the sixth of December, as in the last general election, or on the seventeenth of December, in the election of 1917, without having recourse to sleighs, carriages, or automobiles? And will anyone suggest that all these vehicles are provided by friends absolutely without pay? I do not think so. Well, it is good for those men that have been able to secure vehicles in sufficient numbers to take the electors to the polls, but I think-
May I interject one statement? I may. say that in my election we did not pay one cent to .take electors to the polls in any case; it was all done voluntarily.
I am quite sure my hon. friend is sincere when he makes that statement, 'but probably payment was made and he never knew it. That is how it is done.
I think I can assure my hon. friend that not a cent was paid to anybody.
A person can affirm a positive fact but he .cannot affirm a negative fact. My hon. friend does not know whether that is the case or not.

As far as I am aware
that is the case.

If the committee is satisfied to accept the amendment well and good. Otherwise I am not particularly interested. I believe it is practically impossible to convey electors to the polls, especially now since women are voting, without having to hire a vehicle. There is a defect in this section 12 which should be cured at any rate, and that is the last paragraph.
I should like to know at what my hon. friend is suggesting an amendment. There is nothing at all before the Chair as far as I am aware.
I am presenting an amendment.
If my hon. friend will tell U3 what it is we will appreciate his arguments better.

The amendment
which I propose is as follows:
3a. Section twelve of the said act is amended by striking out the concluding sentence thereof and substituting the following therefor:-
(2) Nothing in this section shall apply
(a)	to the bona fide payment by any elector of the usual fare or of a reasonable charge for the conveyance of himself or any member of his family to or from the polling station, or
(b)	to the payment by a candidate or his election agent for the hire of vehicles at the usual rates current in the locality or of the usual fares payable for transport in any public conveyance, provided that the total amount expended by or on behalf of such candidate for such purposes does not exceed a sum equal to five cents for each elector whose name appears on the list of voters for the electoral district.

There is no section 3;
section 3 is cut out.

Then I move to
add it as section 3.
Elections Act

Where does my hon.
friend come from? The rate he mentions seems very low.

I will give an
explanation. It will be noticed that in the act as at present drafted a man may pay for his own conveyance to and from the polls, but he cannot pay for the conveyance of his wife and family to and from the polls. This was drafted no doubt before the right to vote was given to women. It is quite legal for a man to pay for himself, but not for his wife and family. Therefore, the first part of my amendment desires to secure that right as to the conveyance of the wife and family. The second part of the amendment provides that a candidate or his agent will be able to pay at the usual rates current in the locality for vehicles- to transport electors to the. polls. What amount will be allowed? This is where the five cents for each elector comes in. This may rouse the [DOT] hilarity of members of the committee, but I borrowed it from the English Statutes. If hon. members will read the English Representation of the People's Act, 1918, it will be seen in section 3 or 4, I do not remember which, it is stated that election expenses, outside of other expenses which are declared in the election, shall not be in excess seven pence in the counties and five pence in the boroughs.

Were those the total
elections expenses of a candidate?
No.
For transportation?

These are travelling expenses. This, of course, does not include the personal expenses of the candidate, the making of the lists and so on, I think this allowance of five cents for each elector i3 a right way to proceed. For instance, where there are 10,000 electors in a constituency, the candidate will have a right to spend $500 in that way. If there are 20,000 electors in a constituency, we understand clearly that the candidate should have a right to spend more than in a constituency where there are 10,000 electors and he will be permitted to spend $1,000 in that way. Of course, the rates maybe lowered or raised. This five cent rate is only tentative. If the committee is of opinion that it should be raised or lowered,' it may do so.

The proposition which the hon. member has placed before the committee is a question for Price, Waterhouse

and Company, it is so much involved. He might get some three-cent electors to the polls, and he might find the others to be seven-centers. I do not think we require this at all. If people are interested in the election of their candidate and in the public questions of the day, they will go to the polls if facilities are provided by the establishment of polls where they can go. The hon. member mentions the 6th day of December on which the last election was held. That date worked many inconveniences to the people of the prairie provinces. Today I addressed a letter to the Chief Electoral Officer pointing out that in my electoral district there are many people who are obliged to go ten and fourteen miles to the polls. When the election is held in cold weather, such as the 6th day of December means in western Canada, one can readily understand how impossible it is in many cases for women particularly to go those long distances in order to record their votes. The question was not one of hiring rigs to take the people to the polls but rather one of providing polls in which the people could record their votes. If the hon. gentleman would suggest an amendment to the act which would provide more polling facilities for the people, it would be better than asking for a license for the expenditure of money. The people themselves should be interested enough in public questions and in their candidate to go to the polls and record their approval or disapproval of the various candidates, rather than wait at home in the hope that someone will come to take them to the poll and, perhaps, to record their vote in favour of the person with the first rig that comes along to take them to the poll.
Amendment (Mr. Denis, Joliette), negatived.

I have an amendment which, I think, will come in at this point. I move to amend Bill No. 148 by inserting a new section to be known as section 3:
Section 15 is amended by striking out subsection (1) and inserting the following:
' The afternoon of polling day shall be a general public holiday in Canada."
1 may explain to hon. members that the afternoon on polling day begins at noon. This is an amendment which, I think, ought to meet with some support from the members from Calgary and Winnipeg, as it has been a constant demand by the Trades and Labour Council of Canada in every occasion of late years when they have met the government. The present section, as every hon. member knows, reads:

Elections Act
Every employer shall, on polling day, allow to every elector in his employ at least two additional hours, other than the noon hour for voting-
And it goes on to say that he shall make no deduction from his pay. There is more than one objection to that. One is where there are comparatively large bodies of men employed, a feeling grows up-perhaps it is founded more on apprehension than on experience-that it is not good form to take those two hours off because, if the boss does not want them to go and they insist, when dull times occur, they will be the first to have their services dispensed with. He will not say to them: I will fire you if you take those two hours off. He will say: We are very busy and I hope no one will take advantage of this time to go and vote. I do not know that this has been abused, but there is that feeling amongst the workers.

Does the hon. member not think he is opening the door to just the same difficulty by making a longer time? Is the employer not just as likely to say that the man who takes half a day will be laid off as in regard to the man who is going to take only two hours off?

If the hon. member had
allowed me to finish my argument, he would have found that that objection was met. Let me take another instance. There are factories that work upon what might be called "sequence" labour. I do not know the exact term. There may be a shoe factory with a dozen operatives on machines
11 p.m. working on one part of the shoes and further on another dozen operatives on machines in connection with another part that require the supplies created or handled by the first section. If two or three of the first crowd take two or three hours off, the remaining machines that are, so to speak, behind them, will be more or less idle, and the whole factory will be more or less shut down. That makes it objectionable from the point of view, of course, of the employer in the factory. Then again the old act required that employers should be put into the position of paying their men to go and vote. There are many men who object to that. They say that they do not want someone else to pay for their time while they go and vote. They are quite willing to stand the loss. I meet here the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Stewart, Leeds) who said it would be more objectionable. If in accordance with my suggestion, you make the half day a public holiday, then no one will be paid. They will have to take a half day off because
it will be a public half holiday, and the men will have enough time to go and vote.
What will the penalty be in case any employer wants his men to work and the men do work and draw pay?

If the laws of Canada enact
a public holiday no one is allowed to work.
And what is the penalty?

I must refer the hon. gentleman to the Criminal Code or to the act regarding public holidays to find that out. As the law stands to-day, two or three men may simply insist on going and then they are marked men. The public holiday would-be general; everyone would be free to go in his own time, not being' paid by anyone to do so.

Does the hon. member not
fear that if he made it a public half-holiday the deputy returning officers and election clerks might quit work at noon?

My hon. friend's question is
in line with the argument he advanced a few hours ago when he proposed to closure all amendments to the act. In introducing the amendment I had not in view either the factory worker or the employer but rather the class of people whom I represent, namely, rural workers; and in case the amendment I have suggested is defeated I have another to offer. In sparsely populated sections of the country it is impossible apparently, judging from the experience of the past, for many of the electors to get to the polling stations in two hours time. In the district I represent there are about 125 post offices; and every post office has a nucleus of population around it, or it would not be there. Yet in that district there were only seventy-five or seventy-six polling stations established, and in many cases men and women were compelled to walk or to proceed the best way -they could, in row-boats and launches, five, ten and twenty miles. Let me quote a sentence from a letter I have received, which is typical of various others that have reached me:
With the next federal election in view, wouldn't it be possible to have a polling station nearer here? It is sixteen miles from here to where we voted. Last federal election we had sixteen voters here but only one vote was cast as the rest of the voters wouldn't walk the distance.
I would certainly not ask anyone to walk sixteen miles to vote for me and still less for my opponent, and it is cases of that kind which I think we should make some provision for. The polls should be more frequent and where they are not, then at least men and women should be given a chance to get to the polling
Elections Act

station in ample time to vote. No man Should be expected to leave his work, with the risk of losing his job, in order to vote. I can sincerely say from my own personal knowledge that there were blocks of from twenty-five to a hundred voters who were obliged to travel ten, fifteen and twenty miles to the polling station in my constituency. A logging camp, for instance, is some ten miles from the polling station and the only means of access is by boat. The men knock off two hours earlier at night to comply with the law and by the time they have had supper they are too late to vote when they get to the station. If the boss is a good natured man he may give them the use of his launch; if not the men cannot get to the poll. I would be willing to have the half-holiday' apply only to rural polling divisions if it were felt that such a provision was not needed in the towns.

I think that the
law as it stands at present is adequate. In the two hours allowed for working people to go and vote there is no reason why everybody should not be able to get to the polling station and vote. I have not the least doubt that in two hours it is possible for any elector to vote, and for that reason I shall support the bill as it stands.

The hon. member suggests
that two hours is ample time in which to vote. I gather from that statement that the hon. gentleman has not been much associated with labour people. Let us see how this two hour period works out. Sometimes working men are an hour's ride away from the polling booth and often the Liberal party machine will so organize things that they have from twenty to thirty voters coming into the poll at the moment the working men arrive. Then there will be officers inside the booth swearing every man that comes up to vote and contriving to lose the Bible, so as to consume time and doing all sorts of things to keep the working men back. I have seen two hundred men standing in line outside the polling booth when the poll closed. These had to return to their homes without voting at all because of this practice, and I have seen Liberals swearing old men of seventy to make sure they were of voting age. That is how the two hours works.

I think there is much in
the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Neill). I know that in many instances the two hour rule works a real hardship particularly on working men. I have in mind the situation in my own city where men working in offices and shops five miles from Cal-
gary are obliged to take the street car to get in and consequently many of them are deprived of the opportunity of recording their vote. Especially is this the case where men live in places remote from the city. While the law does provide a two hour interim in which working people shall be allowed to vote, that law is honoured: more in the breach than in the observance. I know of a very strong and wealthy corporation, known to every member of this House, who give the men an hour to vote in, and if they cannot vote in that time they need not vote at all. We should be particularly careful to see that every man who wants to vote gets the opportunity to do so, and I know of no way by which that can be better ensured than by the method proposed by the hon. member..
Is it the intention of the mover of the amendment that the half-holiday shall extend to all the schools throughout the country?
No.

I think it should.
In the province from which I come it is the custom during provincial elections to give the half-holiday and it appears to me to be a good custom. The children get it into their minds that there is something of interest going on and even though they may not be able to understand the questions of the day, in a few years they will be grown up, and this tends to bring them up in an atmosphere of interest in the affairs of the country. I support the amendment even though it does not apply to the schools, as I think it should.
I did not intend it to apply to the schools but I am informed that as a public holiday it would.

I am in favour of the
amendment for much the same reason as I am opposed to the one introduced by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis). It throws the responsibility on the electors themselves. I have always taken the position that men who vote ought to do so in their own time as citizens, but at the same time it is desirable that no employer should 'be allowed to prevent any man from casting his vote. Evidently the two hour provision is inadequate, and for that reason I am strongly in favour of the amendment. It requires the individual to do it in his own time and at his own expense. On the other hand, it prevents an employer putting any obstacle in the way of the employee exercising his franchise.

Elections Act

I desire to say a word
in support of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) in so far as it affects the districts with which I have come in contact. In some parts of this country we have not proper facilities for transportation. Some parts of the western country are not blessed with good roads. Some parts of that country have no means of transportation except by waterways, or by means of isolated railways. This has created a difficulty in some parts of the Dominion because two hours has not proved sufficient for the voter to go to the polls and vote. In that way a good manj' have been deprived of the privilege of exercising their franchise, and I feel that by extending the time to half a day they would be able to record their vote, a privilege which they should be entitled to.
Amendment (Mr. Neill) agreed to: Yeas, 54; nays, 32.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4-Appointment of returning officers.

I would like some explanation as to what the change means. We should not pass these clauses too quickly. I think the section that is proposed to be struck out should be read and also the section taking its place.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The practice is to read the marginal notes.
Will the minister explain the amendment?

Sections 22, 23 and 24 are
replaced by new sections, making very little change. Section 22 provides that the returning officer shall be appointed by the Governor in Council. This provision is changed and the returning officer is appointed by the Secretary of State. That is the only difference.	.

Then there is another feature, is there not, that the election officer is more or less a permanent official? At the present time he is not appointed until after the election is declared. Under this clause he is mor^ or less a permanent officer.
Yes.

Would the minister
think it advisable to make his term longer?
No.

What was found wrong
with the past system where the returning officer
was appointed after the writs were issued? What necessitated the change?

The explanation by the Chief Electoral Officer reads as follows:
That in Canada a general election campaign lasts more than four times as long as in Great Britain is in no way due to geographical considerations, and only in part to the fact that in Canada the lists of voters are prepared during the campaign while in Great Britain they are prepared semi-annually whether or not an election is held. It is to the practice followed in the appointment of returning officers that most of the difference is due. In Great Britain the person who is to act as returning officer in each constituency is fixed by statute or custom; this was once generally the case in Canada, but for many years the selection of returning officers has been made only when the election has been decided upon. If the former Canadian and present British practice were reverted to, the length of the compaign in Canada would be reduced by about half, and the administration of elections would at the same time be greatly improved since prospective returning officers would have an opportunity to familiarize themselves with their duties and districts in advance of the pressure of administrative business.
This is for the purpose of shortening the time between dissolution and an election. How long will it take after dissolution before the election officer would be appointed?
It would take forty-five days.

It was previously sixty
days.
Yes.
It is now fifteen days less.

I can sec some advantages in this provision and some disadvantages. I can see some disadvantages for everybody except the party in power. It will enable the government to bring on an election on shorter notice than could be done at the present time. I think we have all more or less felt that disadvantage at different times in carrying on election campaigns.
The time is too long now.

The party in power
usually has all the advantage anyway. They have all their ammunition ready and the opposition very often have to procure a new candidate, sometimes someone who has never been in politics before. Possibly that is fortunate for him, because he will not have so many sins to answer for. But he has less time to get his organization in shape and run an election.
Is forty-five days too short?

Yes, from the time the election is declared, because they have to call a convention. It is possible to have an election sprung on the people without notice at all. I do not think any of us will be surprised
Elections Act

if we have an election this fall, and if the parties do not prepare for it they will have themselves to blame.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That has been suggested already.

Under this section they will have only .fortydive days to hold their convention, select their candidate, form their organizations and so on. It will be some task. In my constituency we had two representatives previous to 1917. They felt it quite a task to run an election in each county.	At the present time these two
counties form a very large constituency- Victoria and Carleton. I think every constituency in New Brunswick is in pretty much the same position. At one time we had eighteen, to-day we have only eleven ridings. They have grown in area from time to time. I think any man who will undertake to organize a campaign on thirty days' notice will find it very difficult indeed in some of our very large constituencies. For that reason I should like to see some provision made so that the time between dissolution and the date of the poll will not be shortened.

Do you want a year's
notice?
No, reasonable notice.

Mr. Chairman, I agree
with the member for Victoria and Carleton. This country is just about as different from England as could well be conceived. We have no compact little ridings that can be covered in a very brief time and in which organization can be kept going right along, as is possible over there. At the last general election, in order that no one could complain of surprise, three months' notice was given, Two months is certainly not too much. For ridings especially which are large and where all the various preparations have to be made, of which any opposition knows nothing in advance, two months certainly is not too long a period. There is nothing to complain of here. While I am on my feet, may I point out to the government that they are forgetting their professions once more. I can recall how their sensitive consciences were shocked frightfully when this section in its original form was passed. They described as a gross system of party patronage the fact that the Secretary of State appointed the returning officers, and insisted that it be done by the Civil Service Commission. How is it that they have not the commission mentioned here?
Who insisted upon that?
The Liberal party.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Never.

My memory is quite
distinct on the point. This House was aflame with indignation on the part of members of the Liberal party that the government would appoint the returning officers, and they demanded that the appointments be made by the Civil Service Commission so there would be no party patronage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Never in the
world.

The Prime Minister's
memory is short.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say never.
My right hon. friend is mistaken.

No, the Prime Minister
is mistaken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend mean to say that this government demanded that returning officers be appointed by his appointees on the Civil Service Commission when he was in power?

Not this government;
but the Liberal party when in opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend knows it never did-he ought to at. least, if he does not.

The Prime Minister's
indignation, I suppose, is easily accounted for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I' contradict
my right hon. friend flatly, and I ask him to give evidence to prove his assertion.

I remember the indignation of the Liberal party that the government should appoint its own returning officers; scores of members behind the Prime Minister know it too; there is no question of doubt, about it. Now, I object to this facility for rushing on a surprise election. I do not say that the holding of an election this fall would be a surprise. I am not going to complain. Let them go to the electorate as soon as they like as far as I am concerned, and as far as the country is concerned too. But in this Dominion where our distances are so great there should be at least sixty days' notice of an election. I do not ask for more, I do not ask for so long notice as we gave in 1921, but I say it is only reasonable that there should be no facility provided whereby an election can be brought on in less than sixty days.

Elections Act

What section of the
act governs the length of notice that must be given?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The chief electoral officer tells us that under the act as it stands it will take three months, and I am led to believe-

Two months.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING.:	No, three
months under the act as it stands.

We got an answer just
now that it will be two months under the act as it stands, and forty-five days if this section passes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If this passes.

Two months otherwise.
That is what the Secretary of State said just now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I believe I
am absolutely correct in saying that my right hon. friend found to his surprise when the general election came on that it would take three months to carry it out. Everybody knows my right hon. friend said there would be a dissolution in August; he told the country there would be an election then. We were kept campaigning through September, October, November and December, and the country was in a state of turmoil, to the disadvantage of the country and most of all to the disadvantage of my right hon. friend. I think he assumed at the time that if he had an opportunity of traversing this country from one end to the other he would win candidates in every seat, but he came back with a following not as large in numbers as the ministers he had when he went to the country. Forty-five days is the shortest time within wThich a general election can be arranged under- this act. It does not say that fortyffive days will be the time, it may be two months, it may be longer; but the government does feel it is in the public interest and in the interest of the candidates that the country should be spared these interminable periods of turmoil which work to the disadvantage of business generally and to the advantage of no one in particular.

I do not know what is
the matter with the Prime Minister to-night. His mind seems to be in a turmoil. He says I announced a general election in August.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You did, you
stated there was to be an election that year.

An election in August!
Never in the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend intimated in August that there would be an election that year. The election came on in December, as he well remembers.

What I understood the
Prime Minister to say-I suppose I was wrong in this-was that I had announced there would be an election in August.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

I did not announce in
August that there would be an election; it was the first day of September.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The last day
of August.

No, the first day of
September. I would not have bothered correcting so narrow a point as that, but I misunderstood what the Prime Minister meant. But I did not then state when the election would be held, and it was many days before the House was dissolved and an election ordered. I do not remember being informed by anybody that it would take three months, but the time was long for the reason that I was anxious that hon. gentlemen of the Liberal party, who found fault with everything, who were always in a state of indignation no matter what was done, would not have cause to complain that they did not have a chance to persuade the electorate.

We have not had cause to
complain.

No, I do not doubt it.
Certainly there was no advantage to the government in the course it took; but that was the reason. I do remember our being advised from time to time in by-elections-I do not remember in the general election, although perhaps we were-that owing to the new act a longer time was needed than before. I have an amendment which
would come in there, and be known as section 4A, I presume. It is to amend section 30 of the main act, subsection (g), by striking out all the words after the word "Act" in the fifth line. This is only a small amendment, and of importance only to British Columbia. I have here a number of amendments I intended to move. There are nine of them, but I am willing to be a good sport and tear them all up if the House will listen favourably to me on this one small amendment. It is a matter in connection with orientals, but I do not intend to take more than ten minutes in dealing with the subject.
It really strikes me as the base of the autonomous rights of British Columbia, or indeed of any other province. I am not going to take any narrow view. I am not going to introduce into the debate any reasons why we in British Columbia do not want the orientals to vote. That is not pertinent to_ the argument. What I submit is this: British Columbia in virtue of powers conferred on her under the British North America Act has legally prohibited orientals from voting in the province. We have a perfect right to do that, just as we have a right to say if we choose that people with red hair shall not vote. That is the privilege of any province, within the province,

under the British North America Act. It has the right to regulate its own franchise. In case there should be any doubt as to the legality of our action in this regard, this act, which was passed twenty-five or thirty years ago, was tested in every court of Canada and finally taken to the Privy Council, the highest court in the empire, and it was there decided we had such a right. So we may start on that premise, that British Columbia has the right to exclude orientals from voting within the province. At the last election it was found that the late government, possibly by inadvertence, in amending the Dominion Elections Act allowed a certain number of orientals to vote under the provisions of this subsection (g). I will just read what I propose to strike out. Subsection (g) provides:
Persons who, by the laws of any province in Canada, are d squalified from voting for a member of the legislative assembly of such province in respect of race, shall not be qualified to vote in such province under the provisions of this act.
Then comes in this proviso which I propose to strike out:
Provided however that the provisions of this paragraph shall not disqualify or render incompetent to vote any person who has served in the naval, military or air forces of Canada in the late war and who produces a discharge.
He does not need to have been overseas as long as he has a discharge, nor to have been in a theatre of war, although I admit that a number of them went overseas, and a number of them lost their lives.
I want to tell how we dealt with this in British Columbia. We dealt with it thoroughly and efficiently in 1919. Immediately after the close of the war, there was a Provincial Elections Act going through the local legislature, and a deputation of Japanese returned men came to parliament, practically, asking that they be allowed to vote. They met a committee composed partly of members of the government and partly of members of the House for that purpose, nearly all of whom were returned men themselves, and they went thoroughly into the question. The matter was brought up on the floor of the House, and it was decided unanimously not to grant them the vote. The attitude the returned men took was this:	We admit all we owe to
them but it is not in the interest of the two races that this door shall be opened to them. We are determined to exclude them; we can see nothing but trouble and friction arise by giving way on this point. They said "we owe these men gratitude, we owe them some return, but we will show it in some other way." I may say that as far as the mem-

Elections Act
bers from British Columbia are concerned we have since shown it to them in a very practical -spirit indeed. For years past there has been an agitation to restrict the number of Japanese having a license to fish in British Columbia. I fear that we are represented as being prejudiced in that regard, but what did we do. We provided that in the case of these Japanese returned men any restriction would not apply to them. The consequence is that as time goes on the Japanese will be entirely eliminated from the fishing industry of British Columbia except these returned men. These returned men will for all time as long as they live-and I am rather afraid, after they [DOT]die, because their discharges will be passed on to others-will for all time be allowed the privilege of having a fishing license. The privilege at that time would be worth perhaps $1,000 to-day it is worth several hundred dollars. We have allowed that privilege to them but we have not given it to the white returned men. So we say that British Columbia is not so unmindful of the debt she owes to these men and has provided if not a sufficient recompense, at least a very definite recognition of what they have done. It was desirable to compensate them in some way for what they have done, but it would have been a very bad policy for the future of the province to have given them the vote at that time. I again repeat it was unanimously agreed to by the legislature of British Columbia.
Now, I come to the main point of my argument. I have shown that we have, after [DOT]careful consideration, taken the stand in British Columbia that I have indicated. Now here is the point I want to get at: Having done so I claim that it is automatically the Tight of the province of British Columbia to have those same inhibitions transferred into the Dominion franchise when it has been Tecognized from the time of Confederation *down that the provincial franchise is the basis of the franchise in the Dominion. I could go back ten, fifteen, twenty years, and quote the views of the big men of the various parties, but I will not take up the time of the House in doing so. Blake is on record also Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden, the right hon. leader of the present opposition, and last but not least, the present Minister of Justice. They have all gone on record emphatically and in no doubtful language have told us that the provincial franchise is, and must be the only basis and must be [DOT]carried into the Dominion statutes. Now it is a very bitter question in British Columbia, and a very heavy handicap to any party
whose members are in any way connected with the continuing of this position if it is continued. Now I want to address myself not only to the members from the prairies- because their interests are in some sort allied to ours in British Columbia; they are beginning to feel the pinch in some degree as we are-but I want to address myself particularly to the representatives from the province of Quebec for this reason: While their interests are not identical in this regard with ours they are parallel. We live at the opposite ends of this great continent. There is no opportunity for local friction as sometimes arises between Quebec and Ontario. We have many residents in British Columbia that have come from the province of Quebec. We welcome them as good citizens and good friends. We would be very sorry indeed both for their sakes and our own-I admit we are selfish in that particular-to see any action taken here which would form a precedent for the elimination-by means of attack on provincial autonomy-of any of the rights of British Columbia or Quebec. I ask the representatives from Quebec to remember this: If we in British Columbia are to suffer by virtue of being made subject to a majority, that to-morrow will perhaps be the fate of the province of Quebec. If it is right to take from us our inalienable rights to decide what our franchise is, to-morrow there will possibly be an attempt made to interfere with some of the long standing rights of the province of Quebec. For instance I may say we have a very good educational system in British Columbia but will never seek, I hope, to impose that system in place of the method which 'prevails in the province of Quebec.
What about taking from members of any one race their innate rights as human beings to direct their own affairs.

I will deal with that in a
minute. At present I want to conclude my argument in regard to the province of Quebec. Quebec has certain rights peculiar to the province, for instance her land system. We have in British Columbia what we consider is the best land tenure system in the world for simplicity and cheapness. But we know there is a different system in Quebec, and do not seek to impose our system on that province. Quebec, in the matter of dower rights, has also certain distinctive laws of her own. I would ask them to consider that if they do not want these rights interfered with that they themselves should see that our rights in British Columbia are not interfered with either.

Now let me deal with the question, asked by my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth). He asked: What about the inalienable rights of a citizen to vote. It has been held by the very highest courts in the British Empire-and that at least is good enought for me-that the right to vote is not inherent in being a man or even in being a British subject. We do impose conditions even on a white born British subject. We say this man shall not vote until he becomes of a certain age and so on. In England the age for women is thirty. Until quite recently in England there was a property qualification. When I was a young man of twenty-two I was not able to vote in my own country because I did not have some property qualification; I did not rent a house and so on, so it has been held by every court in every part of the British Empire that it is not an inherent right of a British subject to have the right to vote. And we in British Columbia have exercised our right to say who shall and who shall not vote. That right has been accorded to us and affirmed by the Privy Council. I am quite content to rest my argument on that and not to take refuge behind any pretext. The point is simply this: British Columbia under the rights conceded to her by Confederation-or at least inferentially given at Confederation-'because they said that the provincial franchise should govern in the first instance; and certainly it is confirmed by all precedent that has been followed in the last fifty years-has always had the right to decide our own franchise, and that franchise with all its disabilities or inhibitions we ask, should be carried into the Dominion law. That is all we ask in this amendment. It has the unanimous support of every member of every political stripe in British Columbia, and I do hope it will appeal to the House.
